WAGE-AND-HOUR CLAIM FILING DEADLINES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

DECLARATION — WAGE-AND-HOUR CLAIM FILING DEADLINES INFORMATION SHEET
I, Jordan Lee, am completing this information sheet in connection with wages I believe Acme, Inc. owes me from my employment, which is described here, where applicable, as having ended on September 30, 2026.

This information sheet describes California's general civil filing deadlines — statutes of limitations — for the different ways a wage-and-hour claim can be legally characterized once employment has ended: as a claim on a liability created by statute, as a claim founded on a written contract, and as a claim for the waiting-time penalty under Labor Code section 203. It is not a substitute for the DLSE wage claim process or a civil complaint, does not calculate any specific filing deadline for any specific claim, and does not determine that any wages described here are in fact owed. Only the Labor Commissioner, or a court, can determine whether a specific claim was filed within the applicable deadline.

THE THREE-YEAR DEADLINE FOR A CLAIM ON A LIABILITY CREATED BY STATUTE
California's general civil statutes of limitations set a three-year deadline for "[a]n action upon a liability created by statute, other than a penalty or forfeiture." California's highest court has applied this three-year period to an action to recover final wages not paid as required by the Labor Code, and has separately held that the extra pay a statute requires for a missed meal or rest period is itself a "wage or premium pay" governed by this same three-year period, rather than a "penalty" governed by a shorter period — because the obligation to pay it is created by statute rather than sounding purely in penalty.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Within three years: (a) An action upon a liability created by statute, other than a penalty or forfeiture."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 338(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Code of Civil Procedure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=338.)
  "This case presents two issues: first, whether the “one additional hour of pay” provided for in Labor Code section 226.7 constitutes a wage or premium pay subject to a three-year statute of limitations (Code Civ. Proc., § 338) or a penalty subject to a one-year statute of limitations (Code Civ. Proc., § 340)...We conclude that the remedy provided in Labor Code section 226.7 constitutes a wage or premium pay and is governed by a three-year statute of limitations..."
  — Murphy v. Kenneth Cole Productions, Inc., 40 Cal. 4th 1094, 1099-1100 (2007) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5608048/murphy-v-kenneth-cole-productions-inc/)
  Known gap: This is one state's general civil statute of limitations and two California Supreme Court decisions applying it — used as real evidence of how long a statutory wage claim generally has to be filed, not a claim about which state's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim about exactly how many years remain for any specific claim, since accrual dates, tolling, and the specific type of claim asserted can all affect the actual deadline. The two case-law citations below both confirm the three-year period applies to different categories of unpaid compensation (final wages, and meal/rest period premium pay) rather than repeating the same holding, and neither case addresses every Labor Code wage claim by name; this document does not independently verify, claim by claim, that every possible wage-and-hour claim (for example, every minimum-wage or overtime scenario) is treated the same way.

THE FOUR-YEAR DEADLINE FOR A CLAIM FOUNDED ON A WRITTEN CONTRACT
California's general civil statutes of limitations separately set a four-year deadline for "[a]n action upon any contract, obligation or liability founded upon an instrument in writing" (subject to statutory exceptions not addressed here). This is a longer period than the three-year deadline that generally applies to a claim on a liability created by statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Within four years: (a) An action upon any contract, obligation or liability founded upon an instrument in writing, except as provided in Section 336a; provided, that the time within which any action for a money judgment for the balance due upon an obligation for the payment of which a deed of trust or mortgage with power of sale upon real property or any interest therein was given as security, following the exercise of the power of sale in such deed of trust or mortgage, may be brought shall not extend beyond three months after the time of sale under such deed of trust or mortgage."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 337(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Code of Civil Procedure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=337.)
  Known gap: This is one state's general civil statute of limitations, used as real evidence that a longer, four-year filing deadline exists in California law for a claim founded on a written instrument — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that this longer period applies to any particular wage claim. This document did not locate, and does not cite, California case law specifically confirming when a claim to recover wages is treated by a court as "founded upon" a written employment contract for purposes of this four-year period, as opposed to being treated as a claim on a liability created by statute under the three-year period described elsewhere in this document, even where a written employment agreement exists. That characterization can depend on how the specific claim is pled and on the terms of the particular written agreement, and is not resolved by the text of this statute alone; this gap is disclosed rather than filled with an assumed answer.

WHY THE WAITING-TIME PENALTY'S FILING DEADLINE FOLLOWS THE UNDERLYING WAGE CLAIM, NOT THE GENERAL ONE-YEAR PENALTY PERIOD
California's general civil statutes of limitations set a one-year deadline for "[a]n action upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture," unless the statute imposing the penalty prescribes a different limitation. The waiting-time-penalty statute, Labor Code section 203, itself prescribes a different limitation: it states that suit for these penalties may be filed "at any time before the expiration of the statute of limitations on an action for the wages from which the penalties arise." The California Supreme Court has confirmed that this cross-reference means a claim for section 203 penalties is not governed by the general one-year penalty deadline; instead, it is governed by whatever deadline would apply to a claim for the underlying unpaid final wages, and the Court held this is true even when an employee sues to recover the waiting-time penalty alone, without also suing to recover unpaid wages (because, for example, the wages were eventually paid before suit was filed).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Within one year: (a) An action upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture, if the action is given to an individual, or to an individual and the state, except if the statute imposing it prescribes a different limitation."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 340(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Code of Civil Procedure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=340.)
  "Suit may be filed for these penalties at any time before the expiration of the statute of limitations on an action for the wages from which the penalties arise."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 203(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=203.)
  "Section 203(b) sets forth a single limitations period governing all actions to recover section 203 penalties regardless of whether an employee seeks both unpaid wages and penalties or penalties alone. ... Code of Civil Procedure section 340, subdivision (a) provides that a one-year statute of limitations applies to “[a]n action upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture . . . .” ... Thus, if section 203(a) comprised the entire statute, a suit to recover its provided-for penalties would undoubtedly have to be filed within one year of the accrual of the cause of action. However, Code of Civil Procedure section 312 acknowledges the Legislature can, if it so chooses, prescribe a different statute of limitations to govern specific civil actions. To that end, section 203(b) provides, “Suit may be filed for these penalties at any time before the expiration of the statute of limitations on an action for the wages from which the penalties arise.” Actions for final wages not paid as required by sections 201 and 202 are governed by Code of Civil Procedure section 338, subdivision (a), which provides that a three-year statute of limitations applies"
  — Pineda v. Bank of America, N.A., 50 Cal. 4th 1389, 1394-1396 (2010) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2356499/pineda-v-bank-of-america-na/)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutes and one California Supreme Court decision construing them, used as real evidence of how the waiting-time-penalty filing deadline is structured — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim about exactly how many years remain for any specific claim. The three citations below are to two separate statutes (Code of Civil Procedure section 340 and Labor Code section 203, in different codes) and one case construing both, so they are independent of one another rather than restating the same source. This clause does not itself identify which specific deadline (three years, four years, or another period) governs any particular underlying wage claim; that threshold question is addressed by the other authority clauses in this document rather than repeated here.

NO SEPARATE FILING-DEADLINE TEXT FOR A DLSE ADMINISTRATIVE WAGE CLAIM
The Labor Code statute authorizing the Labor Commissioner to investigate wage complaints and hold a hearing on them does not itself state a separate filing deadline — shorter or longer than the general civil deadlines described elsewhere in this document — for a wage claim brought through that administrative process rather than through a civil lawsuit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The Labor Commissioner is authorized to investigate employee complaints. The Labor Commissioner may provide for a hearing in any action to recover wages, penalties, and other demands for compensation, including liquidated damages if the complaint alleges payment of a wage less than the minimum wage fixed by an order of the Industrial Welfare Commission or by statute, properly before the division or the Labor Commissioner, including orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission, and shall determine all matters arising under his or her jurisdiction."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, reviewed for the presence or absence of specific language — used as real evidence that the particular statutory text granting the Labor Commissioner hearing authority does not itself set a separate administrative filing deadline, not as a comprehensive claim that no provision anywhere in the Labor Code or in Division of Labor Standards Enforcement policy could ever impose a different timing rule for some other purpose. This document reviewed only the text of Labor Code section 98 for this point; it does not independently verify the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's internal Policies and Procedures manual, or every other Labor Code section referencing the Labor Commissioner's hearing process, so an administrative-specific timing rule located elsewhere cannot be ruled out from what was verified here. That absence is disclosed rather than treated as a complete negative confirmation.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — WAGE-AND-HOUR CLAIM FILING DEADLINES INFORMATION SHEET
I declare that the information above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes California's general civil filing deadlines for wage-and-hour claims after employment ends, including the three-year period for a statutory wage claim, the four-year period for a claim founded on a written contract, and how the waiting-time-penalty deadline under Labor Code section 203 is tied to the underlying wage claim's own deadline. It is not a DLSE wage claim form or civil complaint, is not filed with any court or agency by completing it, does not itself determine that Jordan Lee is owed any wages by Acme, Inc. or that any specific filing deadline has or has not passed, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.]
